title: People Often Resist a Decision Solely Because of How It Was Made
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership essay synthesizes decades of organizational psychology research on procedural justice to argue that how a decision is made matters as much as — and often more than — what was decided. When team members feel genuinely heard before a decision is finalized, they are far more willing to accept and support the outcome even when it disadvantages them or they disagree with it. The reverse — exclusion, being rushed, or simply being informed after the fact — reliably produces resistance that outlasts the decision itself and drags down execution on unrelated work. The article carefully distinguishes between voice and vote: people do not expect to control every decision, but they insist on being genuinely considered before one is made. The practical implication is that involving team members early in significant decisions — while they can still influence the outcome — is among the highest-leverage tools a leader has, and requires no surrender of final authority.
points: Process justice research is consistent and humbling: the quality of the decision process often matters more to compliance and execution than the quality of the decision itself. Teams judge decisions through the lens of how they were made.

Resistance to a decision is rarely about the decision. It is about what the process communicated about the team member's standing and importance within the organization — a communication that once made is very difficult to undo.

The critical distinction is voice vs. vote: people do not expect authority over every decision but they insist on genuine consideration before one is made. Leaders who conflate the two fail at both: they neither involve people nor make decisions people will execute.

Resistance is rarely vocal. It shows up as disengagement, quiet non-compliance, backroom complaints, and poor execution — and it outlasts the original decision, dragging down performance on completely unrelated work.

All organizations run on discretionary effort — the difference between the minimum and the excellent. Whether team members give that discretionary effort depends more on the decision process they experience than most leaders realize.
quotes: Decades of research in organizational psychology point to a consistent and humbling finding: How a decision is made matters as much as what was decided — and sometimes more. The quality of a decision is often secondary to the decision process.

When people feel they were heard before a decision was finalized, given a genuine opportunity to voice concerns, and treated with respect throughout the process, they are far more willing to accept and support the result, especially when they dislike it or it directly disadvantages them.

When people feel excluded, rushed through, or simply informed after the fact, they resist the decision. This resistance is not always vocal or openly expressed in advocacy. It shows up as disengagement, quiet non-compliance, backroom complaints, and poor execution.

Research has consistently shown that people distinguish clearly between having a voice and having a vote. They do not expect to influence every decision, but they want to be genuinely considered before one is made.

All organizations run on discretionary effort. Whether team members go beyond the minimum, support initiatives they did not choose, and trust leaders through uncertainty depends more on the decision process than many leaders realize.
The bottom line is this: Leaders who remember that the decision process is the message get more done.
